prompt.context: Our client, OOS (Orrington Office Supplies), is a leading manufacturer of office products. In 1991, OOS had sales of $275M. They have strong brands, invest heavily in marketing and advertising, and have grown through product line extensions and four key acquisitions. OOS is organized into 5 autonomous divisions but shares manufacturing and marketing functions. Shared costs (45% of total) are allocated on a percentage-of-sales method. There are three plants currently running at 50% capacity utilization. Analysts predict OOS is a potential acquisition target given its strong balance sheet but weakening earnings. OOS is publicly traded and has little long-term debt.
prompt.question: As a potential investor, how would you improve OOS's profitability?

clarifying_info.q: What are the industry trends for the U.S. office supplies market?
clarifying_info.a: The market grew at 5% CAGR historically. In 1990 and 1991, the market declined at 5% per year. The superstore channel is becoming increasingly critical, gaining 10 share points in the past 2 years. Superstores typically discount products 30% to small retailers/dealers and are aggressively substituting private label products for traditional brand names.

clarifying_info.q: What are OOS's key client/distribution characteristics?
clarifying_info.a: OOS has a broader product line than competitors (12,500 SKUs vs. 4,000-5,000 for competitors). Distribution is 75% wholesalers, 15% superstores, and 10% end customers. The most profitable product is a high-end branded stapler. Staples, Inc. is OOS's largest customer.

exhibits.title: OOS Sales / Profit Trend
exhibits.shows: A chart showing OOS's historical sales and profit trends over time (covering the 1980s into the early 1990s)
exhibits.data: Sales of $275M in 1991; profits declining more steeply than sales in recent years; both metrics visible on a time-series chart

exhibits.title: Overview of OOS Production Plants
exhibits.shows: An overview of OOS's three production plants, including their locations and current SKU capacity
exhibits.data: Three plants: Chihuahua (Mexico), Michigan (US), New Jersey (US); capacity data showing each plant's SKU capacity and current utilization; Chihuahua plant capacity is close to 12,000 SKUs, enabling it to absorb the full 12,500-SKU line (minus 500 SKUs)

exhibits.title: Plant Operating Costs
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of fixed and variable operating costs for each of the three production plants
exhibits.data: Chihuahua: $20M fixed + $4K variable cost per SKU; Michigan: $15M fixed + $7.9K variable cost per SKU; New Jersey: $18M fixed + $8.5K variable cost per SKU

framework: Examine OOS's recent financial performance to diagnose declining profitability (revenue trends, cost structure, fixed vs. variable cost dynamics)
Assess capacity utilization across the three plants and identify consolidation opportunities
Conduct a quantitative profitability analysis of plant consolidation scenarios
Evaluate qualitative/implementation considerations for the recommended path

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, why do the slopes for sales and profits differ as time elapses?
questions.guidance: Two key insights: (1) Profits have been declining more steeply than sales because the business has a high fixed-cost structure — when revenues fall, fixed costs cannot be reduced proportionally, compressing margins faster. (2) Sales did not grow faster than profits during the 1980s likely because OOS grew through acquisitions, which prevented the economies-of-scale gains normally expected in a fixed-cost-heavy manufacturing business.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, qualitatively discuss the options for plant consolidation. Which plant is the most feasible consolidation target?
questions.guidance: The Chihuahua plant has capacity close to 12,000 SKUs. OOS has 12,500 SKUs. Two main options: (A) Close the Chihuahua plant and move all production to the two US plants, or (B) Close the two US plants, discontinue 500 SKUs, and move all production to Chihuahua. Insightful candidates recognize that Option B (consolidate to Chihuahua) is more feasible because Chihuahua has the lowest variable cost per SKU ($4K vs. $7.9K and $8.5K), and the candidate should ask to see cost data (Exhibit 3) before finalizing.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate: (1) How does consolidating all production to Chihuahua change revenues? (2) How does it change production costs? (3) What is the new pre-tax profit?
questions.guidance: Walk through all three calculations: revenue impact from eliminating 500 SKUs, cost savings from closing Michigan and New Jersey, and net profit change. Current pre-tax profit is $25M/year.

math.setup: Current state: $275M revenue / 12,500 SKUs = $22K revenue per SKU. Current production costs = Chihuahua + Michigan + New Jersey. After consolidation: close Michigan and New Jersey, run 12,000 SKUs out of Chihuahua.
steps: Revenue impact: Eliminate 500 SKUs x $22K/SKU = $11M revenue reduction. New revenue = $275M - $11M = $264M

Current production costs: Chihuahua = $20M + ($4K x 4,500 SKUs) = $20M + $18M = $38M; Michigan = $15M + ($7.9K x 5,000 SKUs) = $15M + $39.5M = $54.5M; New Jersey = $18M + ($8.5K x 3,000 SKUs) = $18M + $25.5M = $43.5M; Total current production costs = $136M
Post-consolidation production costs: Chihuahua only = $20M + ($4K x 12,000 SKUs) = $20M + $48M = $68M
Cost savings = $136M - $68M = $68M reduction in production costs
Net profit impact = Cost savings - Revenue loss = $68M - $11M = $57M improvement
New pre-tax profit = $25M + $57M = $82M (more than tripling current profits)
math.answer: New annual pre-tax profit = $82M, up from $25M — an increase of $57M (229% improvement).

recommendation: OOS should eliminate 500 SKUs and consolidate all production to the Chihuahua plant, raising annual pre-tax profits from $25M to $82M — a more than 3x improvement.
The consolidation captures $68M in annual cost savings, more than offsetting the $11M revenue loss from discontinuing 500 low-priority SKUs.
risks: Union relationships: If Michigan or New Jersey plants have organized labor, closing them requires careful negotiation and may involve severance obligations.
Implementation timeframe: The transition cannot happen overnight; production continuity must be maintained during the changeover.
Distribution and warehousing disruption: A carefully-developed transition plan is needed to avoid service failures during the consolidation.
Culture and morale: Communicating the change properly is critical; employee morale at all locations (including Chihuahua) must be managed.
SKU rationalization risk: Eliminating 500 SKUs may affect key customer relationships if any discontinued products are important to major accounts like Staples, Inc.
next_steps: Develop a detailed implementation and transition timeline for closing Michigan and New Jersey plants.
Transition to a strong central purchasing department, replacing smaller local purchasing operations.
Analyze which 500 SKUs to discontinue — prioritize eliminating the least profitable and lowest-volume products.
Engage proactively with union representatives and employee groups at the plants to be closed.
Develop a distribution and warehousing transition plan to maintain service levels throughout consolidation.
